687.title: Guru Hargobind's gurpurab
687.hook: remembered with the two swords of miri and piri
687.howItsDone: On Guru Hargobind's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some communities display gatka; Sikhs remember his two swords of miri and piri and the Akal Takht he founded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baoli, and your line: eighty-four steps. Today we skip ahead, past the fifth Guru, to his son.

A boy, about eleven by tradition's count, has just lost his father. Not to an accident. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the man who built the Harmandir Sahib and gathered the Granth, has died in custody in Lahore; Sikhs remember it as his shaheedi, his martyrdom. The Sikhs are grieving and afraid. And when the boy becomes the sixth Guru, he does something new. Tradition says he asks for two swords, and he puts on both. Today: Akal Takht.
screen: `A BOY WHO HAS LOST HIS FATHER.` → `A MARTYRDOM IN LAHORE.` → `HE PUTS ON TWO SWORDS.`

segments.voice: Guru Hargobind was born near Amritsar. You've met his birth already: the shabad of Guru Arjan's joy when his son arrived. After his father's execution he became Guru, and the two swords he wore became a lasting idea in Sikh life. One sword was miri: worldly power, responsibility in the world, the duty to protect. The other was piri: spiritual authority, the life of devotion and the Name. The words echo two titles: mir, a ruler, and pir, a spiritual guide. The point wasn't two separate lives. A Sikh holds both at once. As Sikhs often explain it, devotion without courage can abandon the weak, and power without devotion turns cruel. The two swords keep each other honest. He gave the idea a building. Facing the Harmandir Sahib, he raised a platform called the Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One. The Harmandir is where the Word is sung; the Akal Takht is where the community gathers to decide, and act. Even today, they stand looking at each other across the same courtyard. Guru Hargobind kept horses and armed followers, and fought battles with Mughal forces. He was also, tradition remembers, a man of deep devotion who kept the kirtan going morning and evening. The two outer swords of the Khanda emblem are often read the same way. His gurpurab is marked with kirtan, and in some places with displays of gatka, the Sikh martial art. Two swords, one Guru.

segments.voice: If you can, stand, feet planted, shoulders back, chin level; if you can't, sit as tall as you can. Feel your weight evenly on both sides, one for your duties in the world, one for your inner life, and breathe in strength, breathe out stillness. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing like that.
Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One Guru Hargobind raised facing the Harmandir Sahib, where the community gathers to decide and act.
Your line: two swords. Courage and devotion, each one worn every day. See you tomorrow.

688.title: Guru Har Rai's gurpurab
688.howItsDone: On Guru Har Rai's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some Sikhs mark it by planting trees, tending gardens or serving in health care, remembering the seventh Guru's gardens and medicine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akal Takht, and your line: two swords. Today, his grandson, who kept the swords and was remembered for flowers.

Sikhs tell a story about a boy walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe. As he passes, the hem catches a flower and snaps its stem. The petals fall. His grandfather sees it and says something gentle: if you wear a robe like that, you have to carry it carefully. The boy is said to have held his robe gathered close for the rest of his life, so it would never break a flower again. That boy became the seventh Guru. Today: Har Rai.
screen: `A ROBE CATCHES A FLOWER.` → `THE GRANDFATHER'S GENTLE WORD.` → `A ROBE HELD CLOSE FOR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Rai was the grandson of Guru Hargobind, and he succeeded him as the seventh Guru while still young. He made his home at Kiratpur, in the hills of Punjab. The story of the flower is tradition, not a record, but it fits how Sikhs remember him: a gentle man, careful with living things. At Kiratpur, he's remembered for gardens: fruit trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs. Tradition says he kept a dispensary there, where medicines were made and given freely to anyone who came. He also kept the armed horsemen his grandfather had begun, but his years as Guru were largely peaceful. One story about his medicine reaches all the way to the Mughal court. Tradition tells that Dara Shikoh, a son of the emperor Shah Jahan, fell gravely ill, and the court's physicians couldn't find a remedy. A rare herb was needed, and it was sent from Guru Har Rai's stores. Dara recovered. The striking part is who got the medicine: a prince of the same ruling house that had executed the Guru's great-grandfather, Guru Arjan. The healer didn't ask which side the patient was on. Sikh tradition reads that as the teaching heard all through the Gurus' hymns: the One is in everyone, so care goes to everyone. His gurpurab is marked with kirtan and langar, and some gurdwaras and families mark it with things he'd recognize: planting trees, tending gardens, or volunteering in clinics. The healer, remembered by healing.

segments.voice: If there's a plant near you, bring it some water now, slowly, and watch the soil darken; if not, picture one you love, or a tree you pass each day. As you water, think of one living thing you could be more careful with, a person, an animal, a place, and gather your robe close, so to speak. If you pray, Waheguru can go in with the water.
Har Rai, the seventh Guru, remembered on his gurpurab with gardens, herbs, and medicine given freely, even to the emperor's son.
Your line: the healer. Gardens, herbs, and a robe held close. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab
689.hook: remembered with care for the sick at Bangla Sahib
689.howItsDone: On Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab, Sikhs gather at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi and elsewhere for kirtan and langar; many take water from Bangla Sahib's pool to the sick and serve the unwell in his memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Har Rai, and your line: the healer. Today, his son, the youngest of all the Gurus.

In the middle of New Delhi, there's a white gurdwara with a golden dome and a large pool. Day and night, people come with bottles to take its water home to someone sick. Its langar hall serves meals from morning to night. And the whole place is built around the memory of a child, who came to Delhi because an emperor summoned him, and stayed to look after the sick. Today: Bangla Sahib.
screen: `A WHITE GURDWARA IN NEW DELHI.` → `BOTTLES OF WATER FOR THE SICK.` → `THE MEMORY OF A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Krishan was the younger son of Guru Har Rai. Before his father died, he named the boy as the eighth Guru; tradition says he was about five. Some objected, including his older brother, Ram Rai, who had gone to the Mughal court and won favor there. The emperor Aurangzeb summoned the young Guru to Delhi. There he stayed at the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh, a Rajput noble. That house is now Gurdwara Bangla Sahib: bangla means bungalow. While he was there, an epidemic struck the city; tradition usually names smallpox, and some accounts say cholera. Tradition says the child Guru went out among the sick, of every faith, giving water and comfort and care. He caught the disease himself and died, still a child; tradition says he was about eight. Asked who would follow him, tradition says, his last words were Baba Bakale: the next Guru is at Bakala, which proved to be Guru Tegh Bahadur. The Sikh Ardas, which you learned line by line this year, remembers him in a single line. In paraphrase: remember Guru Har Krishan, at the sight of whom all suffering departs. Today, the pool at Bangla Sahib is where people take water for the sick, in his memory. His gurpurab is marked there with kirtan and langar, and some Sikhs visit or serve the sick that day. A very short life, remembered for care that walked toward the sickness instead of away from it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you know who's sick, recovering or worn out, and picture them clearly. Hold them with care, and let one small, real kindness for them come to mind: a message, a meal, a ride, an hour of company. If you pray, you can say the Ardas line for them in your own way, or just Waheguru.
Bangla Sahib, the Delhi gurdwara built around the bungalow where the child Guru stayed and cared for the sick in an epidemic.
Your line: the child healer. A short life, and a long memory. That's day six hundred eighty-nine.

690.title: The first installation
690.hook: the day the Adi Granth was first placed in the Harmandir in 1604 is celebrated in late summer
690.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate the Pehla Prakash, the first installation of the Adi Granth in the Harmandir Sahib in 1604, with kirtan, illuminations and a procession at Amritsar, and with special programs in gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bangla Sahib, and your line: the child healer. We've walked through the Gurus' days. Now, two days for the book itself.

A passport. A house deed. A letter from someone who's gone. Nobody tosses papers like that into a bag; they get carried with two hands. In 1604, Sikhs carried a book that way: the words of the Gurus and saints, gathered over years and copied by hand, brought for the first time into the building raised to house it. Who carried it? Where did it sit? And where did the Guru sit? Today: Adi Granth.
screen: `HELD WITH TWO HANDS.` → `A BOOK COPIED BY HAND.` → `CARRIED IN FOR THE FIRST TIME.`

segments.voice: By the early 1600s, Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, had gathered the hymns of the first five Gurus, along with those of Hindu and Muslim saints whose words shared the Gurus' vision. Bhai Gurdas wrote them out as scribe. The finished volume was called the Adi Granth, the first book. In 1604, it was carried into the newly built Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar and opened there for the first time. Sikh tradition remembers the scene. Baba Buddha, a revered elder who had known Guru Nanak himself, carried the Granth on his head. He was appointed its first granthi, the one who reads it and cares for it. The Granth was placed on a raised seat, and Guru Arjan sat below it. The Guru, at a lower level than the book: that small detail says a great deal about what was coming. Then the Granth was opened at random, as it still is each day, for the first hukamnama, the day's command. Tradition gives the first one as a shabad of Guru Arjan in Raag Suhi, on Ang seven eighty-three. In paraphrase: the Lord Himself stood up to complete the work of His saints; the Lord came to do the work. Sikhs mark this day as the Pehla Prakash, the first opening, in late summer. At the Harmandir Sahib it's celebrated with kirtan, lights and a great procession. And every morning since, in that same building, the Granth has been carried in and opened again: the word, installed.

segments.voice: Take a book that matters to you, a scripture, a gutka, a book of poems, a book someone gave you, and hold it in both hands, pausing before you open it. Then open it slowly, wherever it falls, and read just one line as if it were addressed to you today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before you open it.
Adi Granth, the first book of the Gurus' hymns, carried into the Harmandir Sahib in 1604 by Baba Buddha, with Guru Arjan seated below it.
Your line: the word installed. Held high, and opened every morning. Day six hundred ninety, done.

691.title: Guruship to the Granth
691.hook: the day in 1708 the Guru Granth Sahib became Guru is marked each autumn
691.howItsDone: Sikhs mark Gurta Gaddi Divas each autumn with kirtan, readings and processions, especially at Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib in Nanded, where Guru Gobind Singh conferred guruship on the Granth in 1708.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adi Granth, and your line: the word installed. A hundred and four years after that first opening, the book received something more than a place.

A community led by a living teacher meets a hard question sooner or later: what happens after? Who guides it when the teacher is gone? For the Sikhs, that question came to a head in 1708, far from Punjab, at Nanded in the Deccan, by the Godavari river. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, had been gravely wounded. His four sons had all died before him. The Sikhs around him asked who would guide them next. Today: Gurta Gaddi.
screen: `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER?` → `NANDED, 1708.` → `WHO WILL GUIDE US NEXT?`

segments.voice: Gurta Gaddi means the throne of guruship: gaddi is the seat, the cushion of authority, and gurta is the office of the Guru. Sikh tradition remembers what happened at Nanded in 1708. Guru Gobind Singh placed five coins and a coconut before the Granth, the same sign used when one Guru installed the next, and bowed to it. He declared that after him there would be no human Guru. The Granth itself, now called the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the Guru: for Sikhs, not only a holy book, but the Guru, living in the Word. Tradition says that not long before, at Damdama Sahib, the Granth had been completed with the hymns of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. So the Word was whole. Sikhs also speak of the Guru Panth, the community of the Khalsa, as carrying the Guru's authority together, guided by the Granth. After the Ardas, sangats often sing a couplet that says: by the command of the Timeless One the Panth was established; all Sikhs are commanded to accept the Granth as Guru. That couplet comes from later Sikh writings rather than the Granth itself, but it puts the teaching in a line sangats sing together. What follows is simple and large. In Sikh understanding, every Sikh, anywhere in the world, has direct access to the Guru. No human successor stands between a Sikh and the Guru. Just the Word, opened each morning, read each night. The Gurta Gaddi Divas is marked each autumn with kirtan, readings and processions, especially at Hazur Sahib in Nanded.

segments.voice: If there's a Guru Granth Sahib or a gutka near you, bow to it, the way Sikhs do on entering the darbar; if not, picture the Granth on its raised seat, covered in cloth, a granthi waving the chaur above it, and bow your head toward that picture, slowly. Let the bow mean: I'm ready to listen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you rise.

Your line: the eternal guru. The Word, whole, and in every Sikh's reach. See you tomorrow.

692.title: Looking back: the daily banis
692.hook: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, heard in order
692.howItsDone: Many Sikhs say the Japji, Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Savaiye in the early morning, often with Chaupai and Anand Sahib, then Rehras at dusk and Kirtan Sohila before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurta Gaddi: in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh passed the guruship to the Granth, and your line, the eternal guru. Today we turn around and look back at the year.

Six banis. One day. A Sikh home before dawn: a kettle, a dark window, a voice already reading. By breakfast, several prayers have passed. At dusk, another. At bedtime, one more, with the lights low. This year you met each of those prayers on its own, block by block, sometimes for weeks. Today you hear them as they're lived: in order, one day long. Looking back: the daily banis.
screen: `SIX BANIS, ONE DAY.` → `MORNING, DUSK, NIGHT.` → `HEARD IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Start in the dark. Amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, is when the Sikh code of conduct asks a Sikh to rise, bathe and begin. After the Japji comes the Jaap Sahib, which Sikhs know as Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise, all short lines and quick meters. You met its line in the spring: namastvam akaale, salutation to the One beyond time. Then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, ten verses under the heading by Your grace: the poet has seen monks, yogis and mighty kings by the thousand, and says all of it is worth nothing without love. Then, in some homes, the Benti Chaupai, a prayer for shelter: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa, give me Your hand and keep me safe. Then Guru Amar Das's Anand Sahib, the song of bliss, which opens with a cry of joy: anand bhaiaa meree maae, I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. That's the morning. Then the day itself: work, traffic, dishes, people. The banis don't ask anyone to leave it. They frame it. At dusk, as work ends, Rehras, the evening prayer. It opens with So Dar, the door where the Creator sits and cares for all. And last, at bedtime, Kirtan Sohila, five short hymns, beginning jai ghar keerat aakheeai: in the house where the Creator's praises are sung. The same hymns are sung at funerals, so the close of a day and the close of a life share one song. Notice what the order does. Praise first, before anything has happened. Shelter for the hours ahead. Joy. A door at dusk. A song for sleep. The whole day, held between words.

segments.voice: Say one line from each, slowly, aloud or under your breath, with a full breath between: namastvam akaale; tav prasad, by Your grace; hamree karo hath dai rachhaa; anand bhaiaa meree maae; so dar; jai ghar keerat aakheeai. If a line won't come, say it in English, and let that be enough. Then rest in the quiet after the sixth.
Looking back. Turning around near the top of the year to see the daily banis together: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, from before dawn to bedtime.
Your line: the day, held. Words at both edges, and the day between. Until tomorrow.

693.title: Looking back: the long hymns
693.hook: Sukhmani, Asa di Var, Barah Maha and the ninth Guru's saloks
693.howItsDone: Many Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily or in family gatherings, gurdwaras sing Asa di Var before sunrise, the Barah Maha is read on Sangrand, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the close of a full reading of the Granth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the daily banis, Jaap at dawn to Sohila at night, and your line: the day, held. Today, the long hymns.

Some prayers fit in a breath. Others take an hour and more, and people make room for them anyway. In some Sikh families, when someone is ill or a home is starting something new, relatives gather on the floor to read Sukhmani Sahib together, start to finish, passing it along. In gurdwaras before sunrise, ragis are already singing a ballad that runs until the sky goes pale. Long hymns ask for time, and often company. This year gave you four. Looking back: the long hymns.
screen: `SOME PRAYERS FIT IN A BREATH.` → `SOME TAKE AN HOUR, TOGETHER.` → `FOUR LONG HYMNS.`

segments.voice: First, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's psalm of peace, in Raga Gauri: twenty-four ashtpadis, each opening with a salok and then eight stanzas. Some read it whole; some read a part each day. Its refrain names the whole hymn: sukhmani sukh amrit prabh naam, the jewel of peace is God's ambrosial Name, the resting place of the devotees' minds. This path spent a hundred days on it, longer than on anything else this year. Second, Asa di Var, Guru Nanak's ballad for dawn. A var was a hero's ballad, sung about kings and battles. Guru Nanak took the form and turned it inward: twenty-four pauris, with saloks of Guru Nanak and Guru Angad, and in the gurdwara Guru Ram Das's chhants sung between them. Its first salok is gratitude: balihaaree gur aapne, a sacrifice to my Guru, a hundred times a day. Third, the Barah Maha, Guru Arjan's twelve months in Raga Majh. In the old Punjabi form, a woman longs for her absent beloved as the seasons turn; here the longing is the soul's, for God. It opens with people separated by their own deeds, asking in mercy to be united, and Sikhs read it in gurdwaras on Sangrand. Fourth, the saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, near the very end of the Granth: short, calm couplets about a world that passes and a Name that stays. One says the wise person frightens no one and fears no one. Four long hymns, four moods: peace, gratitude, longing, steadiness. And this week has been a look back of its own: the Gurus' gurpurabs, the first installation, the Granth made Guru, and the daily banis.
screen: `SUKHMANI: THE JEWEL OF PEACE.` · `ASA DI VAR: A BALLAD AT DAWN.` · `BARAH MAHA: TWELVE MONTHS OF LONGING.` · `THE NINTH GURU'S STEADY SALOKS.` · then, large: `THE LONG HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Peace, gratitude, longing or steadiness: pick the one you need today, and find a few lines of it in a gutka, a gurbani app, or simply in memory. Read them slowly, twice, and let one phrase come back now and then, like a tune you can't shake. If you pray, you can let those lines carry your prayer.
Looking back. Four long hymns side by side: Sukhmani's peace, Asa di Var's gratitude, the Barah Maha's longing, and the ninth Guru's steady saloks.
Your line: the long hymns. Some things are worth the whole hour. Another week, done.
